attribution.note: Marcus's own sentence in his own post, stated as his conclusion.

semantics.note: The sentence says where the left-handed failures come from: language understanding, not drawing capacity. The normalised version keeps that exclusive contrast and its scope.

contract.note: The plain reading is ordinary: successful reworded prompts show the model can render the scene, and the cause of failure must be isolated. It is not stretched either way.

evidence.note: OpenAI's 2023 statement about itself says better captions improved prompt following. It is general background and does not test the February 2024 handedness failures or isolate their cause.

reviews.rationale: The only item is a company disclosure about general prompt following. The packet has no controlled same-model comparison that separates misreading the handedness request from rendering limits or sampling effects. Neither the support condition nor the contradiction condition is met.

attribution.note: Marcus quotes his own earlier coauthored writing with Davis and endorses it. It is his claim.

semantics.note: Keeps the scope (brief Marcus–Davis experiments) and the wording 'complete failure.' It is a report of what an experiment found.

contract.note: Reading 'complete failure' as a basic biological error in the reported run is ordinary and generous to the speaker. Scoring rests on authenticating the reported continuation, which is fair.

evidence.note: A June 2021 preprint by other researchers discusses the juice example and cites Marcus and Davis. It does not independently preserve the original run. It also suggests GPT-3 held the relevant knowledge, which cuts against a 'complete' failure, but it does not settle the record.

reviews.rationale: No independent record of the original prompt and continuation is in the packet. e1 relies on Marcus and Davis and uses a different framing, so it neither authenticates the run nor shows it was misreported. The outcome stays open.

attribution.note: Marcus's own sentence in his own post.

semantics.note: 'That's why' ties the difficulty to the preceding point that systems use statistics as a stand-in for understanding. The normalised version keeps 'always' and the example.

contract.note: Reading it as recurring difficulty with rare compositions, caused by frequency priors, is a fair, ordinary reading. It requires evidence of both the difficulty and the cause, which matches the speaker's words.

evidence.note: An October 2023 preprint finds that Stable Diffusion 2.1 does worse on reversed relations as the familiar relation becomes more frequent in training. This is partial support for the frequency mechanism, but it covers one system and is correlational.

reviews.rationale: e2 supports a frequency-prior effect in one model. The packet does not show it across representative systems over time, and it does not separate understanding from other limits. Nothing contradicts the claim. The support condition is only partly met.

attribution.note: This is Marcus's own rebuttal. The critic's objection is only paraphrased as the thing he is answering.

semantics.note: The checkable core is that Google Images readily shows many people drawing left-handed. 'Nonsense' is his judgement on the critic's point, and the narrowed scope is kept.

contract.note: Reading 'a few seconds' as easy to find and 'lots' as numerous is ordinary. Excluding the separate inference about training data is fair.

reviews.rationale: The packet has no evidence items. No archived or contemporaneous Google Images results from February 2024 were found, so the claimed abundance can be neither confirmed nor refuted.
